extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers interested in the history of advertising (historians, advertising scholars, cultural historians)
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter-style historical account of methods, conventions, and regulations used to obtain publicity in ancient Greece and Rome and in the Middle Ages (public criers, wall inscriptions, placards, broadsides, touts, statutory rules). Contains examples and primary-text quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the public crier as the primary advertising medium
rubrics_metrics.description: The public crier (prcecones / town-criers) perambulated towns announcing sales, rewards, proclamations, and other notices; in medieval and earlier times the crier was often the chief organ for obtaining publicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Greek and Roman criers, medieval criers with horns; criers might combine duties of crier and auctioneer; criers kept audiences attentive by joking and loud proclamation (Apuleius's auctioneer-crier). Statutes regulated their duties and privileges (e.g., France, town charters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accompany proclamations with musical pitch or correct tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the Greeks a public crier would not be allowed to proclaim laws unless accompanied by a musician, who could give him the proper pitch and expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Ensure accurate pronunciation and oratorical power; implies that for formal/legal proclamations the delivery quality was considered important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear, specific identifying details in public notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Proclamations should 'clearly describe the marks by which [a person] may be recognised' and include names and sundry particulars so no one can plead ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Venus gives Mercury a book with Psyche's name and particulars so the crier can prevent false excuses; guidance is to include identifying marks and names in lost-person/reward notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer rewards (or threats) to motivate action
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicity was often coupled with an offered reward (or, alternatively, with curses/threats) to induce desired behaviour—e.g., rewards for finding runaway slaves or returning lost animals; curses inscribed on lead invoked punishment for offenders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: reward inscriptions exhumed from Thebes; Greek temple imprecations (defixiones) naming offenders and threatening divine vengeance; Roman and mythic literary examples where rewards include material pay or symbolic rewards (kisses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Select high-traffic locations for postings and wall inscriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Painted notices and inscriptions were placed 'in the most frequented parts'—under porticos, by baths, on walls where passers-by and waiting crowds would see them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Pompeii walls, portico of the baths as advertising stations; guidance is to prefer places of great resort to maximize audience exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use painted wall inscriptions and whitewashed 'albums' on houses
rubrics_metrics.description: Both Greeks and Romans used a piece of wall whitened (album) to receive inscriptions; advertisements were painted in black or red directly on walls or painted on smooth surfaces between pilasters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes: inscriptions were often hasty with indifferent spelling; some notices were scratched rather than painted; album served as a designated ad-space on houses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concise formulaic inscriptions for events and entertainments
rubrics_metrics.description: Event notices (e.g., gladiatorial games, theatre) employed short, formulaic Latin inscriptions stating the performers, date, and nature of the spectacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: inscriptions from Pompeii listing the aedilis, family of gladiators, dates, and spectacles; include dates/times and types of entertainment in compact form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affix short notices to premises and post detailed bills at advertising stations
rubrics_metrics.description: Those with premises to let or sell affixed a short notice to the house itself while posting more detailed bills at advertising stations or in public places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'lUico aedes venales' painted on doors; auctioneers provided fuller particulars on larger placards or in public advertising locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe property fully in auction and rental notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Auctioneers and landlords used descriptive phrases (e.g., 'Villa bona beneque edificata') and provided full details of premises in larger placards to inform potential tenants/buyers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: include quality descriptors, tract/amenities, lease terms and applicable dates as in Roman examples (leases from specific ides/dates, duration in years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Carry and display product samples (taste/sampling) when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Wine-criers carried large wooden measures of wine and made samples available for passers-by to taste as part of the advertisement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: French wine-criers per charters would go from tavern to tavern with samples; sampling was an accepted tactic to attract immediate purchases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe statutory/regulatory rules governing criers and proclamations
rubrics_metrics.description: Criers and proclaimers were subject to statutes prescribing who could cry certain goods, fees due to criers, times/days they could cry, and exclusive rights (e.g., Assizes of Jerusalem gave appointed criers exclusive right to proclaim auctions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: French charter of Louis VII (1141) and later statutes: only twelve criers in a province, criers entitled to fees, schedule limits (no crying on certain religious days), Assizes: exclusive proclamation rights with penalties for unauthorised proclamations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use touts/doorsmen and vocal street-selling to attract customers
rubrics_metrics.description: Shopkeepers employed touts or men at the door shouting and vociferating to attract passers-by ('What d'ye lack?'), sometimes supplemented by insistent persuasion and free samples or food.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: medieval and early modern touting in Cheapside and other streets; practice included persuasive door-calls and occasional free luncheons for regulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit printed broadsides and shop placards once printing exists
rubrics_metrics.description: With the invention of printing, printers and booksellers produced broadsides and placards to multiply advertisements and announce new works or sales (e.g., Caxton's circa-1480 broadside announcing sale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: early printed posters by Caxton (five by seven inches) giving where to get the work and price; Parisian printers later proclaimed cheapness within early books; guidance: use printed handbills to reach a wider audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertise new books and works visibly at the point of sale
rubrics_metrics.description: Booksellers placarded their shops with titles of new books and the University compelled booksellers to advertise new manuscripts in their shop windows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: shop-window notices, lists of available books, and brief exhortations inside books (distichs) to attract buyers; guidance: display titles and price information at the point of purchase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rhetoric/versification or brief slogans to reassure about price or quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Printers and sellers sometimes used short verses or slogans in Latin or vernacular to allay purchasers' fears about price or to extol quality (e.g., 'Ne fugite ob pretium: dives pauperque venite'—'Don't run away on account of the price').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: employ catchy, reassuring couplets or short mottoes to communicate value and encourage buyers.
